business: Acutaas (called Ami Organics until 2025, based in Surat) makes the chemical building blocks that drug companies turn into medicines (pharma intermediates). Think of a company making engine parts for car makers: it doesn’t sell cars, but cars can’t be built without it. It is also growing a newer business in specialty chemicals for batteries and semiconductors.

metrics.label: Revenue CAGR (4 yrs)
metrics.meaning: Sales grew from ₹520 cr to ₹1,339 cr, about 27% a year on average.

metrics.label: Profit CAGR (4 yrs)
metrics.meaning: Profit went from ₹72 cr to ₹356 cr, but dipped to ₹43 cr in FY24, so growth was uneven.

metrics.label: ROCE
metrics.native: Return on all capital in the business
metrics.meaning: About ₹29 earned a year on every ₹100 invested in the business.

metrics.label: ROE
metrics.meaning: About ₹21 of profit a year on every ₹100 of shareholders’ money.

metrics.label: Debt-to-equity
metrics.meaning: Almost no debt. It holds about ₹198 cr more cash than it owes.

metrics.label: Interest coverage
metrics.meaning: Profit covers interest more than 100 times over. Not a concern.

metrics.label: Cash conversion
metrics.meaning: About ₹80 of real cash for every ₹100 of reported profit (FY25–FY26), right at the comfortable line. Worth watching.

metrics.label: P/E (FY26)
metrics.native: Price ÷ last year’s profit per share
metrics.meaning: Investors pay about ₹89 for every ₹1 of last year’s profit per share. The broad sector average is about ₹46, but close peers such as Sai Life (~95) and Anthem (~79) are also priced high.

metrics.label: P/E (TTM)
metrics.native: Price ÷ last 4 quarters’ profit per share
metrics.meaning: On the latest 4 quarters’ profit, investors pay about ₹73 per ₹1. This is the more current figure, and the one the scenarios and calculator use.

metrics.label: Promoter pledge
metrics.native: Founders’ shares given as loan collateral
metrics.meaning: No pledged shares, so no risk of lenders force-selling them in a fall.

positives: Fast growth: in FY26, sales rose 33% and profit rose 124%.
Wider margins: operating margin rose from about 23% to 36%.
Almost no debt, with net cash in hand.
Management raised FY27 guidance to about 30% revenue growth (from 25%) and a 38–40% EBITDA margin.
concerns: Expensive: P/E of about 89, roughly double the broad sector average (~46), though close contract-manufacturing peers also trade at 80–95. The stock is up about 135% in a year, so high expectations are already in the price.
The newer specialty chemicals business (battery and semiconductor chemicals) shrank about 20% in the latest quarter. The diversification story isn’t proven yet.
Very volatile: it moves about 3.4× as much as the Nifty, and fell 10% in a single day in April 2026.
Promoter stake fell from about 41% after the IPO to 32.7%, mostly through new share issues (dilution) plus some promoter sales in 2025. It has been unchanged for the last 5 quarters.
questions: Will the company keep raising money by issuing new shares? Each issue means existing shareholders own a little less.
Is the margin jump permanent (better product mix) or temporary (a few large orders)?
Can it grow 25%+ a year for many years? Paying ₹73–89 for every ₹1 of profit assumes roughly that.

lesson.title: What does paying ₹73 for ₹1 of profit mean?
body: Suppose a shop earns ₹1 lakh a year and you pay ₹73 lakh for it. Even if its profit grows 25% every year, in 5 years it will earn about ₹3 lakh a year: three times as much.
If buyers then pay only ₹30 for every ₹1 of profit (still above the sector average), the shop is worth about ₹92 lakh. Profit tripled, but your money grew only about 26%, roughly 4.7% a year.
That’s why a great company and a great investment are not the same thing. The price you pay matters.
The calculator below starts from Acutaas’s real numbers. Move the sliders to see how growth, years and what investors pay per ₹1 of profit change the price.

quiz.q: Acutaas’s P/E is about 73 (based on the last 4 quarters). What does that tell you?
options: Investors are paying about ₹73 for every ₹1 of yearly profit per share
You will get your money back in 73 years
quiz.explain: P/E compares today’s price with yearly profit per share. It doesn’t predict growth, and it isn’t a payback period: the company keeps most of its profit instead of paying it out to you.

items.title: Q2 FY27 results: revenue +43%, profit +71% vs the same quarter last year
items.why: Revenue was ₹437 cr and profit ₹123 cr. EBITDA margin rose to about 40% from 31%, so the business is earning more on every rupee of sales.
items.not_conclude: One strong quarter isn’t a trend, and margins this high may not last if the product mix changes.
items.source: Company results (27 Oct 2026); Angel One, Indian Chemical News

items.title: FY27 guidance raised to ~30% revenue growth and 38–40% EBITDA margin
items.why: Management expects the rest of the year to stay strong, citing its order pipeline.
items.not_conclude: Guidance is a promise, not a result. Check it against actual results next quarter.

items.title: Specialty chemicals revenue fell about 20% in the quarter
items.why: Growth came almost entirely from pharma intermediates. The newer battery and semiconductor business, a big part of the long-term story, went backwards.
items.not_conclude: New businesses are often lumpy early on. One weak quarter doesn’t mean the strategy failed, but watch the next few.

items.title: South Korea semiconductor-chemicals plant inaugurated ahead of schedule
items.why: Adds capacity for the specialty business.
items.not_conclude: A new plant is spending now; revenue from it comes later, if demand is there.

items.title: Shareholding: foreign funds up to 22.6% (from 21.6%), mutual funds 14.4%, promoters unchanged at 32.66%
items.why: Big investors added slightly during the quarter.
items.not_conclude: Fund buying is a weak signal. Funds are often wrong and can sell just as quickly.

items.title: Share price jumped over 14% on results day
items.why: Shows how much the market liked the results.
items.not_conclude: A price jump isn’t new information about the business. When the price rises faster than profit, the bar for the next quarter rises too.

scenarios.intro: No one can honestly put a buy/sell percentage on a stock. Instead, here is what could happen to ₹1 lakh invested today at ₹3,787 a share, under three different futures.

cases.name: Growth slows
cases.desc: Profit keeps growing, but more slowly, and investors stop paying a premium.

cases.name: Roughly as planned
cases.desc: Growth close to what management is aiming for; the premium shrinks a bit.

cases.name: Everything goes right
cases.desc: Fast growth continues and investors stay excited.
